summary:
Nicaragua does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct or transgender identity. Article 204 of the Criminal Code, added by socially conservative legislators to a bill originally drafted to protect women from rape, made it an offence punishable by up to three years' imprisonment to "induce, promote, propagandize, or practice sex among persons of the same sex in a scandalous manner"; President Violeta Chamorro signed it in July 1992 and the Supreme Court rejected a constitutional challenge brought in November 1992 when it ruled in March 1994. The provision's vagueness also made it usable against LGBT-rights organising and sexual-health work. The language was dropped when a new Penal Code took effect on 1 March 2008, and same-sex conduct has not been criminalised since. The age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender, and sexual offences under Criminal Code articles 168, 170, 172 and 175 are gender-neutral.

Family law excludes same-sex couples. The National Assembly approved a revised Family Code in June 2014 that limits marriage, stable partnerships and adoption to heterosexual couples; it took effect on 8 April 2015, and several organisations filed an action of unconstitutionality against it, with no outcome recorded in this inventory. Article 72 of the Constitution defines marriage and stable unions as resting on voluntary agreement between a man and a woman, and same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the legal benefits and protections available to opposite-sex married couples. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 holds that states parties to the American Convention on Human Rights must grant same-sex couples access to all domestic family-law institutions including marriage; no Nicaraguan implementation is recorded.

Discrimination protections exist but are framed around sexual orientation. Article 315 of the Penal Code, covering offences against labour rights, punishes employment discrimination based on "sexual option" by up to one year in prison. Article 3(l) of Law N° 820 prohibits discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds in the HIV and AIDS context, and Article 36(5) of the Penal Code makes sexual-orientation discrimination an aggravating circumstance when any criminal offence is committed. No transgender-specific hate-crime aggravator is stated in the sources. Ministerial Resolution 671-2014, adopted by the Ministry of Health and repealing Resolution 249-2009, bars discrimination in access to health services in public and private health units on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression.

The US State Department's 2023 human rights report on Nicaragua documents a police and parapolice campaign of harassment, intimidation and violence against perceived regime enemies that authorities did not investigate or prosecute, and lists violence or threats against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer or intersex persons among the significant violations. The official US assessment therefore places anti-LGBTI abuse inside a climate of state impunity.

Documented violence is recorded year by year. Programa Feminista La Corriente reported 67 assaults, 1 hate crime or murder and 2 suicides in 2021; 39 assaults, 3 hate crimes and 1 suicide in 2022; 35 assaults, 2 hate crimes, 1 murder, 1 suicide, 2 sexual assaults and 1 extortion in 2023; and, for the first two quarters of 2024 as reported in April 2025, 13 assaults, 5 hate crimes and 1 missing person. These are raw counts from a single NGO with no population denominator, so they indicate documented events rather than a rate. Across those years trans women are identified as the most targeted group, with gay men second in 2022, and state police are named among the aggressors, tied with family members in number of assaults in 2022; in 2021 acquaintances and state police each committed 10 documented aggressions, occurring mainly in the street or in homes.

A 2012 survey by the Center for Justice and International Law counted 53 aggressions between 1999 and 2011, among them 15 murders comprising 10 gay men, 4 transgender people and 1 lesbian, with the true figure expected to be higher because many victims do not report attacks to police. The sources state that violence against the LGBTQ community is generally culturally accepted and legally unenforced, and that attacks go largely unreported out of fear of retaliation and poor legal outcomes. Media reporting is largely suppressed, much of the media having been restricted since the 2018 protests, which limits coverage of LGBT issues.

On 22 March 2011 Nicaragua joined a United Nations Human Rights Council joint statement calling on states to end violence, criminal sanctions and related human-rights violations committed against individuals because of sexual orientation or gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
Public opinion is largely opposed to legal equality. A Pew survey conducted 9 November to 13 December 2013 found 77% opposed to same-sex marriage, 16% in favour and 7% unsure, while the 2017 AmericasBarometer showed 24.5% support. Both figures are more than several years old and measure opinion on marriage rather than attitudes to transgender people specifically.

The post-April-2018 protest crackdown left at least 325 dead and more than 2,000 injured per the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, according to Amnesty International in May 2019. The same account records journalist Miguel Mora describing being beaten by a pro-government mob and being targeted partly for being gay, an instance of homophobia operating inside the political repression rather than a trans-specific incident.

Visibility is uneven: gay men are generally more visible in public than lesbians, who often socialise privately, and an annual Gay Pride celebration has been held in Managua around 28 June since the country's first public pride festival in 1991. The Freedom and Marriage Global Barometers page for Nicaragua records no documented finding for this jurisdiction.
localsOnly:
Residents have a statutory route against workplace discrimination: Article 315 of the Penal Code punishes discrimination based on "sexual option" in employment by up to one year in prison, and Article 36(5) treats sexual-orientation discrimination as an aggravating circumstance in any criminal case. The sources do not state that either provision is framed to cover gender identity.

Residents also have a stated non-discrimination standard in health care. Ministerial Resolution 671-2014 requires public and private health units to refrain from discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, and Article 3(l) of Law N° 820 covers sexual orientation in the HIV and AIDS context. No youth-specific care-access findings are recorded.

Resident-facing family law is restrictive: the Family Code in force since 8 April 2015 limits marriage, stable partnerships and adoption to heterosexual couples, and Article 72 of the Constitution anchors marriage and stable unions to voluntary agreement between a man and a woman. Reporting channels are weak in practice, since the sources describe attacks as largely unreported out of fear of retaliation and dismal legal results, and note that media coverage of LGBT issues has been constrained since the 2018 protests.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the outcome of the actions of unconstitutionality filed against the 2014 Family Code is not recorded in this inventory, so the current constitutional status of that challenge is unknown.

Unresolved: no Nicaraguan implementation of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 is recorded, and the inventory does not show whether any legislative or executive step toward recognition has been taken.

Unresolved: the sources do not state how a relationship involving a transgender person would be classified under the Family Code or Article 72 of the Constitution, which define marriage by reference to a man and a woman. Whether legal sex recognition would change that classification is not sourced here.

Unresolved: the violence figures are raw counts from one NGO and one 2012 survey, with no population denominator and no general homicide baseline in the inventory, so they cannot be converted into a rate or compared with background violence. The sources themselves describe the totals as undercounts because of non-reporting.

Unresolved: no trans-specific hate-crime aggravating provision is stated; the Penal Code Article 36(5) aggravator described is framed on motivation by discrimination based on sexual orientation. Whether gender identity is covered elsewhere in sentencing law is not sourced.

The Freedom and Marriage Global Barometers page for Nicaragua records no documented finding for this jurisdiction, so no independent verification of the legal position is available from that source.
